question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14081725/assets/d42e9c6ed71f06c2dec273a91d3a4cfbdf5c58095be9370285d7987d38f7b5a6.png)

Which integral  expression gives the arc length of the curve $h(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+t\,k$ from  $t=0$ to $t=2\pi ?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we find ${h}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{h}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,k \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+1\,k \\ ‖{h}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t+1} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }‖{h}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: Which integral expression gives the arc length of the curve $r(t)={t}^{3}\,i+3t\,j+{t}^{4}\,k$ from  $t=2$ to $t=5?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{4})\,k \\  & =3{t}^{2}\,i+3\,j+4{t}^{3}\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(3{t}^{2})^{2}+(3)^{2}+(4{t}^{3})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9{t}^{4}+9+16{t}^{6}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{2}^{5}‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t={\int }_{2}^{5}\sqrt{16{t}^{6}+9{t}^{4}+9}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:

Find the arc length of the curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+2t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-2t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩$
from  $t=1$ to $t=2.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+2t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡2t-2t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)⟩ \\  & =⟨4t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,,4t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(4t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)}^{2}+{(4t\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{t}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡t+16{t}^{2}{sin}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{t}^{2}} \\  & =4t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $t>0$ for $t\in [1,2].$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{1}^{2}‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}4t\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{t}^{2}{|}_{1}^{2} \\  & =2(4-1) \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
Find the arc length of the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2},\,4,\,{t}^{2}⟩$
from  $t=0$ to $t=2.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,\,0,\,2t⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(2t)}^{2}+0+{(2t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{8{t}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\,t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $t\ge 0$ for $t\in [0,2].$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{2}‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2\sqrt{2}t\,\text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{2}({t}^{2}){|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =4\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Computing the Arc Length of a Three-Dimensional Spatial Curve
question.problem:
Find the arc length of the curve $f(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t+t\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}{t}^{2}⟩$
from $t=1$ to $t=3.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we find ${f}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{f}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+t\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t-(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\sqrt{3}t⟩ \\  & =⟨t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,t\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\sqrt{3}t⟩ \\ ‖{f}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(t\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\sqrt{3}t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{t}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)+3{t}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{t}^{2}} \\  & =2t\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $t>0$ for $t\in [1,3].$

Therefore, the arc length of the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{1}^{3}‖{f}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}2t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{2}{|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =9-1 \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Sine
question.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{9\cdot (1-{x}^{2}/9)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}/9}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/3)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

 

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{3})}^{2}.$  

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{3}.$ Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=3\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/3)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot (3\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{x}{3})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|x|\sqrt{3{x}^{2}-1}}=\int \frac{\sqrt{3}}{|\sqrt{3}x|\sqrt{(\sqrt{3}x)^{2}-1}}\text{d}x.
$$

This integral now resembles the basic one for $\text{arcsec},$

$$
\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\text{d}u=\text{arcsec}(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $\sqrt{3}x.$

So, let's substitute $u=\sqrt{3}x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\sqrt{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{3{x}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{\sqrt{3}}{|\sqrt{3}x|\sqrt{(\sqrt{3}x)^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{3}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\text{d}u) \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\int \frac{\text{d}u}{|u|\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\text{arcsec }u+C \\  & =\text{arcsec}(\sqrt{3}x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

question.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent,

$$
\int \frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\text{d}u=\operatorname{arctan}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $4{x}^{2}=(2x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=2x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

Before substituting, we use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

| $x$ | $0$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $2$ |

Using the above, we can now write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{1+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{\text{d}x}{1+(2x)^{2}} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{1+{u}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{\text{d}u}{1+{u}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡u{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(0) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14082094/assets/f74f28bf0b5bf2208b3cebf837c667cf9a9ae737d7eb758708a98548ffca8e3a.png)

Which of the following gives the length of the curve $y=4{sin}^{2}⁡x$ on $[-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}],$ as shown above?
question.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=4{sin}^{2}⁡x,$ $a=-\frac{\pi }{2},$ and $b=\frac{\pi }{2}.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=4\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)
$$

Substituting ${f}^{′}(x)=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)$ into the arc length formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{1+{[{f}^{′}(x)]}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{1+16{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating the Arc Length of a Smooth Curve Using the Arc Length Formula
question.problem: Compute the arc length of $y=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}+{e}^{-x})$ for $x\in [0,\operatorname{ln}⁡2].$
question.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}+{e}^{-x}),$ $a=0,$ and $b=\operatorname{ln}⁡2.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x})
$$

Now, let's compute $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}} & =\sqrt{1+{[\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x})]}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{4}({e}^{2x}-2+{e}^{-2x})} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}({e}^{2x}+2+{e}^{-2x})} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}{({e}^{x}+{e}^{-x})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}+{e}^{-x})\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}+{e}^{-x})$ to the formula for the arc length, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}({e}^{x}+{e}^{-x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}){|}_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[({e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-{e}^{-\operatorname{ln}⁡2})-({e}^{0}-{e}^{-0})] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[2-\frac{1}{2}-0] \\  & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$
